chapters.title: Living in a Rural Area
chapters.description: Talk about rural and city life and learn the simple present tense.

lessons.title: Rural Life and the Simple Present Tense
lessons.summary: Learn words for describing village and city life, and use the simple present tense to talk about daily habits, general truths, and timetables.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Many Ethiopians live in **rural areas** (the countryside, like villages near Ambo or Assosa), while others live in **urban areas** (big cities like Addis Ababa).

In this unit you will talk about daily life in the village and the city. To do this, you need the **simple present tense** — the tense we use most often to describe what people *usually* do every day.

sections.title: What You Will Learn
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Use **vocabulary** to describe rural and urban life.
- Form the **simple present tense** correctly (add **-s** for he/she/it).
- Use the simple present for **habits**, **general truths**, and **timetables**.
- Avoid the most common mistakes ESL learners make with this tense.

sections.title: The Simple Present Tense
sections.body:
We use the **simple present tense** for actions that happen regularly or that are always true.

**Rule 1 — The base verb:** For *I, you, we, they*, use the plain verb.
- I **drink** tea every morning.
- They **live** in a village.

**Rule 2 — Add -s/-es for he, she, it:** This is the most important rule!
- Tolosa **goes** to school five days a week.
- Aster **prepares** breakfast.
- He **watches** films. (verbs ending in -ch, -sh, -s, -x, -o add **-es**)

**Rule 3 — Negatives and questions** use **do/does**:
- I **do not (don't) like** noise.
- She **does not (doesn't) like** the city.
- **Do** you exercise? / **Does** he work here?

Note: after *does* / *doesn't*, the main verb has **no -s** (Does she **go**? — not *goes*).

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.body:
Read about Ato Gebeyehu's family and notice the **-s** endings:

*"Aster **gets** up early. She **prepares** breakfast and **gets** the children ready for school. Belete **milks** the cows and **feeds** the cattle. In the evening, the family **dines** together."*

Now compare singular and plural:
- Belete **milks** the cows. (he → verb + s)
- Adanech and Alemitu **fetch** water. (they → base verb, no s)

**Timetable use:** *The train **leaves** at seven o'clock.* *The restaurant **opens** at 7:30 tonight.* We use simple present for fixed schedules, even though they are in the future.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.body:
- **Forgetting -s:** ❌ *He go to school.* ✅ *He **goes** to school.*
- **Adding -s after does:** ❌ *Does she likes it?* ✅ *Does she **like** it?*
- **Double negative:** ❌ *She doesn't likes nothing.* ✅ *She **doesn't like** anything.*
- **Using -s with I/you/we/they:** ❌ *They lives here.* ✅ *They **live** here.*

sections.title: Memory Tip
sections.body: Remember **"HE, SHE, IT — add an S!"** Say it like a small song. If the subject is one person or thing (he, she, it, Aster, the dog), the verb almost always ends in **-s**.

sections.title: Practice
sections.body:
Write the correct form of the verb.

1. My mother (cook) ______ injera every day.
2. We (live) ______ in Addis Ababa.
3. (Do/Does) ______ Tolosa play football?
4. The bus (leave) ______ at 6 a.m.
5. He (not / like) ______ the noisy city.

**Answers:** 1. cooks  2. live  3. Does  4. leaves  5. does not like (doesn't like)

sections.title: Key Vocabulary
sections.body: Words from the reading passage about rural and urban life.

glossary.definition: the countryside; areas with villages and farms, not cities.
a city or town with many people, buildings, and traffic.
dirty air, water, or land caused by smoke, gases, or waste.
very crowded and full of people or traffic.
easy to use or do; saving you trouble or time.
to send out gas, smoke, or sound.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
- The **simple present** describes habits, general truths, and timetables.
- Add **-s/-es** to the verb for **he, she, it**.
- Use **do/does** for negatives and questions; the main verb stays in its **base form**.
- **Rural** = countryside (fresh air, quiet); **urban** = city (more services, more pollution).

flashcards.front: When do we add -s to the verb?
flashcards.back: With he, she, it (one person or thing): She goes, He works.

flashcards.front: What tense for timetables? 'The train ___ at 7.'
flashcards.back: Simple present: The train leaves at 7.

options: She go to school every day.
She goes to school every day.
She going to school every day.
She gone to school every day.
questions.explanation: With 'she' (he/she/it), we add -s to the verb: She goes.

questions.prompt: Complete: He ______ like the noisy city.
questions.explanation: For he/she/it we use 'doesn't' (does not) to make a negative.
After 'does', the main verb has no -s: Does she like films?
Congested means overcrowded, full of people or traffic.

questions.prompt: According to the unit, one advantage of city life is that ______.
options: there is access to medical care and services
questions.explanation: The passage says cities have complete facilities such as transport, education, and health care.

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the simple present for a TIMETABLE?
options: The plane arrives in five minutes.
questions.explanation: Timetables and fixed schedules use the simple present: The plane arrives in five minutes.

chapters.title: History of the Calendar
chapters.description: Learn about calendars and use the simple past tense to talk about the past.

lessons.title: Calendars and the Simple Past Tense
lessons.summary: Explore the history of the Ethiopian and Gregorian calendars and learn to form the simple past tense for finished actions.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
A **calendar** helps us count days, months, and years. The **Ethiopian calendar** has 13 months — twelve months of 30 days and one short month called *Pagume*. The **Gregorian calendar**, used in most of the world, has 12 months.

To talk about history — things that **happened before** — we use the **simple past tense**.

sections.title: What You Will Learn
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Talk about calendars and how people **counted** time.
- Form **regular** past verbs (add **-ed**) and learn **irregular** verbs.
- Make **negatives** and **questions** in the past with **did/didn't**.
- Use the **colon** correctly.

sections.title: The Simple Past Tense
sections.body:
We use the **simple past** for actions that started and finished in the past.

**Regular verbs:** add **-ed**.
- walk → **walked**, modify → **modified**, adopt → **adopted**.

**Spelling notes:**
- verb ending in **-e**: just add **-d** (live → lived).
- consonant + **-y**: change y to i, add -ed (study → studied).
- short verb ending in vowel + consonant: double the consonant (stop → stopped).

**Irregular verbs** do not follow the rule — you must learn them:
- go → **went**, is/am → **was**, are → **were**, have → **had**, make → **made**, name → **named** (regular).

**Negatives and questions** use **did**, and the main verb goes back to its **base form**:
- I **did not (didn't) go**.
- **Did** you **see** the calendar?

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.body:
Read this short history and notice the past verbs:

*"The Ethiopian calendar **got** its origin from the ancient Egyptians. Later, people **modified** it for the Coptic Christians. The Gregorian calendar **was** named after Pope Gregory XIII, who **changed** the older Julian calendar."*

- **got** = irregular past of *get*
- **modified** = regular (y → i + ed)
- **was** = past of *is*
- **changed** = regular (-d)

**Colon example:** *The Ethiopian calendar has thirteen months: twelve long months and one short month.* The colon (**:**) introduces a list or explanation.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.body:
- **Adding -ed to irregular verbs:** ❌ *He goed home.* ✅ *He **went** home.*
- **Keeping past tense after 'did':** ❌ *Did you went?* ✅ *Did you **go**?*
- **was/were confusion:** ❌ *They was happy.* ✅ *They **were** happy.* (I/he/she/it = was; you/we/they = were)
- **Forgetting spelling change:** ❌ *He studyed.* ✅ *He **studied**.*

sections.title: Memory Tip
sections.body: After **DID**, the verb goes back to the **DICTIONARY (base) form** — "DID + base." The word *did* already shows the past, so the main verb does not need to.

sections.title: Practice
sections.body:
Put the verb into the simple past.

1. Yesterday I (visit) ______ my grandmother.
2. The Egyptians (modify) ______ their calendar.
3. We (go) ______ to the market.
4. (Do) ______ you see the new calendar?
5. She (not / be) ______ at home.

**Answers:** 1. visited  2. modified  3. went  4. Did  5. was not (wasn't)

sections.title: Key Vocabulary
sections.body: Useful words about calendars and time.

glossary.definition: a system that shows the days, weeks, and months of a year.
the place or point where something begins or comes from.
to change something a little to make it better or fit a need.
to start to use or accept something officially.
a year with one extra day (or, in Ethiopia, an extra day in Pagume).

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
- The **simple past** describes finished actions in the past.
- **Regular** verbs add **-ed**; **irregular** verbs (go→went, is→was) must be learned.
- Use **did/didn't** + **base verb** for questions and negatives.
- A **colon (:)** introduces a list or an explanation.
- The **Ethiopian calendar** has 13 months.

flashcards.back: Did you see it? (did + base verb)
It introduces a list or an explanation.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct past tense: 'Yesterday she ______ to school.'
questions.explanation: Regular verbs add -ed: walked.

questions.prompt: What is the past tense of 'go'?
questions.explanation: 'Go' is irregular: go → went.
After 'did', the verb returns to its base form: Did you go home?
Plural subjects (students = they) use 'were'.

questions.prompt: How many months does the Ethiopian calendar have?
questions.explanation: The Ethiopian calendar has 13 months: twelve of 30 days and one short month (Pagume).

questions.prompt: Which sentence uses the colon correctly?
options: I bought three fruits: apples, bananas, and oranges.
questions.explanation: A colon introduces a list after a complete idea: 'I bought three fruits: ...'.

chapters.title: Road Safety
chapters.description: Stay safe on the road and learn modal verbs and giving advice.

lessons.title: Road Safety and Modal Verbs
lessons.summary: Learn road-safety vocabulary and use modal verbs (must, should, have to, can) to give rules and advice.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Every day, students cross busy roads on the way to school. **Road safety** means knowing the rules that keep us safe: looking both ways, using the **zebra crossing**, and obeying **traffic lights**.

To talk about rules and advice, we use special helping verbs called **modal verbs**: *must, should, have to, can*.

sections.title: What You Will Learn
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Use **road-safety vocabulary** correctly.
- Use **modal verbs** to express **rules** (must), **advice** (should), and **ability** (can).
- Give safety advice in clear, correct sentences.

sections.title: Modal Verbs for Rules and Advice
sections.body:
**Modal verbs** are helping verbs that come **before** the main verb. The main verb stays in its **base form** (no -s, no -ed).

- **must** = a strong rule or obligation. *You **must stop** at a red light.*
- **must not (mustn't)** = it is forbidden. *You **must not cross** when the light is red.*
- **should** = advice (a good idea). *You **should look** both ways.*
- **shouldn't** = advice not to do something. *You **shouldn't run** across the road.*
- **have to / has to** = a rule (like must). *Drivers **have to wear** seat belts.*
- **can / can't** = ability or permission. *Pedestrians **can cross** at the zebra crossing.*

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.body:
Here are safety rules written with modals:

*"When you walk to school in Addis Ababa, you **must** use the footpath. You **should** look left and right before crossing. You **must not** play on the road. Drivers **have to** slow down near schools. You **can** cross safely at the zebra crossing."*

Notice every modal is followed by a **base verb**: must **use**, should **look**, have to **slow**.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.body:
- **Adding 'to' after must/should/can:** ❌ *You must to stop.* ✅ *You **must stop**.* (but: *have **to** stop* is correct)
- **Adding -s to the main verb:** ❌ *He should looks.* ✅ *He **should look**.*
- **Adding -s to the modal:** ❌ *She musts go.* ✅ *She **must** go.* (modals never change)
- **Using 'don't must':** ❌ *You don't must run.* ✅ *You **must not** run.*

sections.title: Memory Tip
sections.body: Think: **MODAL + BARE VERB.** Modals are like a strict teacher — they never change shape and the verb after them stays plain. Only *have to* uses the word *to*.

sections.title: Practice
sections.body:
Choose the best modal.

1. You ______ stop at a red light. (rule) ______
2. You ______ look both ways before crossing. (advice) ______
3. You ______ play football on the road. (forbidden) ______
4. Drivers ______ wear seat belts. (rule) ______
5. Pedestrians ______ cross at the zebra crossing. (ability/permission) ______

**Answers:** 1. must  2. should  3. must not (mustn't)  4. have to / must  5. can

sections.title: Key Vocabulary
sections.body: Important road-safety words.

glossary.definition: a person who is walking, especially on a road or street.
black-and-white stripes on a road where people can cross safely.
lights (red, yellow, green) that control cars and people.
a path beside a road for people to walk on; a pavement.
a sudden bad event, such as a car crash, that is not planned.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
- **Modal verbs** (must, should, have to, can) come before a **base verb**.
- **must / have to** = strong rule; **must not** = forbidden.
- **should / shouldn't** = advice.
- **can / can't** = ability or permission.
- Stay safe: use the **zebra crossing**, watch the **traffic lights**, and walk on the **footpath**.

flashcards.front: Which modal means a strong rule?
Correct the error: 'You must to stop.'

flashcards.back: striped place on a road where people cross safely

questions.prompt: Choose the best advice: 'You ______ look both ways before crossing.'
questions.explanation: 'Should' is used to give advice (a good idea).
After a modal, use the base verb with no 'to': must stop.

questions.prompt: Which sentence means something is forbidden?
questions.explanation: 'Must not' (mustn't) means it is not allowed / forbidden.

questions.prompt: A 'pedestrian' is a person who is ______.
questions.explanation: A pedestrian is a person who is walking.

questions.prompt: Complete: 'Drivers ______ wear seat belts. It is the law.'
questions.explanation: 'Have to' shows a rule or law (like 'must').
Modals never take -s and are followed by the base verb: She must cross.

chapters.title: Endemic Animals in Ethiopia
chapters.description: Learn about Ethiopia's unique animals and use comparative and superlative adjectives.

lessons.title: Endemic Animals and Comparing Things
lessons.summary: Discover Ethiopia's endemic animals and learn comparative and superlative adjectives to compare them.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Ethiopia is home to special **endemic animals** — animals found *only* in Ethiopia and nowhere else in the world. Examples are the **Walia ibex**, the **Gelada baboon**, the **Ethiopian wolf**, and the **Mountain nyala**.

To describe and compare these animals, we use **comparative** and **superlative adjectives**.

sections.title: What You Will Learn
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Use vocabulary about **animals** and **wildlife**.
- Form **comparative** adjectives (to compare **two** things).
- Form **superlative** adjectives (to compare **three or more** things).
- Use *than* and *the* correctly.

sections.title: Comparative and Superlative Adjectives
sections.body:
We compare things using **comparatives** and **superlatives**.

**Short adjectives (1 syllable): add -er / -est**
- fast → **faster** → the **fastest**
- tall → **taller** → the **tallest**

**Adjectives ending in -y: change y to i**
- heavy → **heavier** → the **heaviest**

**Long adjectives (2+ syllables): use more / most**
- beautiful → **more beautiful** → the **most beautiful**
- dangerous → **more dangerous** → the **most dangerous**

**Irregular:** good → **better** → the **best**; bad → **worse** → the **worst**.

**Use 'than' with comparatives:** *The wolf is **faster than** the baboon.*
**Use 'the' with superlatives:** *The Walia ibex is **the rarest** animal.*

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.body:
Compare some Ethiopian animals:

- The **Gelada baboon** is **bigger than** the Ethiopian wolf. (compare two)
- The **Ethiopian wolf** is **rarer than** the Mountain nyala. (compare two)
- The **Walia ibex** is one of **the rarest** animals in the world. (compare many)
- The Gelada is **more social than** most monkeys. (long adjective → *more*)

Notice: short word → *bigger*; long word → *more social*; with the top one → *the rarest*.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.body:
- **Using 'more' AND '-er' together:** ❌ *more faster* ✅ *faster*
- **Forgetting 'than':** ❌ *The wolf is faster the fox.* ✅ *The wolf is faster **than** the fox.*
- **Forgetting 'the' with superlatives:** ❌ *It is rarest animal.* ✅ *It is **the** rarest animal.*
- **Wrong form of irregulars:** ❌ *gooder, more good* ✅ *better*

sections.title: Memory Tip
sections.body: **Short word, short ending (-er/-est). Long word, extra word (more/most).** Count the syllables: one syllable → add -er/-est; two or more → use more/most.

sections.title: Practice
sections.body:
Write the comparative or superlative.

1. The cheetah is (fast) ______ than the lion.
2. The Walia ibex is one of (rare) ______ animals in Ethiopia.
3. This lake is (beautiful) ______ than that one.
4. Mount Ras Dashen is the (high) ______ mountain in Ethiopia.
5. Today the weather is (good) ______ than yesterday.

**Answers:** 1. faster  2. the rarest  3. more beautiful  4. highest  5. better

sections.title: Key Vocabulary
sections.body: Words about animals and wildlife.

glossary.definition: found naturally in only one place and nowhere else in the world.
a group of animals or plants that are similar and can have young together.
the natural home where an animal or plant lives.
at risk of dying out completely (very few are left).
animals and plants that live in nature, not kept by people.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
- **Comparatives** compare **two** things; **superlatives** compare **three or more**.
- Short adjectives: **-er / -est**. Long adjectives: **more / most**.
- Use **than** with comparatives and **the** with superlatives.
- **Endemic** animals like the **Walia ibex** live only in Ethiopia.

flashcards.back: found only in one place in the world
the natural home where an animal lives

options: The cheetah is more fast than the lion.
The cheetah is faster than the lion.
The cheetah is fastest than the lion.
The cheetah is fast than the lion.
questions.explanation: Short adjective: fast → faster, used with 'than'.
Superlatives use 'the' + adjective + -est: the rarest.
Long adjectives use 'more': more dangerous.

options: is found only in one place in the world
questions.explanation: Endemic means found naturally in only one place.
'Good' is irregular: good → better → best.

options: The Walia ibex is more rarer than the nyala.
The Walia ibex is the most rare animal.
The Walia ibex is rarer than the nyala.
The Walia ibex is rarest than the nyala.
questions.explanation: Never use 'more' with '-er'. Use 'rarer than' for comparing two.

chapters.title: Diary
chapters.description: Learn to write a personal diary using the past tense and time expressions.

lessons.title: Writing a Diary and Using Time Expressions
lessons.summary: Learn how to write a personal diary entry, using the past tense and time expressions to describe your day.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
A **diary** (also called a *journal*) is a private book where you write about your day — what you did, saw, and felt. Writing a diary helps you practise English every day.

We write a diary mostly in the **past tense**, and we use **time expressions** like *yesterday, in the morning, after that* to put events in order.

sections.title: What You Will Learn
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Understand the **format** of a diary entry (date, greeting, events, feelings).
- Use the **past tense** to describe your day.
- Use **time expressions** and **sequence words** to order events.
- Express your **feelings** with simple adjectives.

sections.title: How to Write a Diary
sections.body:
A diary entry usually has:

1. **The date** at the top (e.g. *Monday, 27 June 2026*).
2. A greeting like *Dear Diary,*.
3. The **events** of the day, in order, in the **past tense**.
4. Your **feelings** about the day.

**Time and sequence words** keep your writing clear:
- *In the morning, in the afternoon, in the evening*
- *First, then, after that, next, finally*
- *Yesterday, today, last night*

**Feelings adjectives:** *happy, excited, tired, sad, proud, worried.*

Because a diary describes things that already happened, most verbs are in the **simple past**: *I **woke** up, I **went**, I **felt**.*

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.body:
Here is a model diary entry:

*Monday, 27 June 2026*

*Dear Diary,*

*Today **was** a busy day. **In the morning**, I **woke** up early and **helped** my mother fetch water. **Then** I **went** to school and **learned** about endemic animals. **After that**, I **played** football with Dawit. **In the evening**, I **felt** tired but **happy**. **Finally**, I **did** my homework and **went** to bed.*

Notice the **past verbs** (was, woke, helped, went) and the **sequence words** (in the morning, then, after that, finally).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.body:
- **Mixing tenses:** ❌ *Yesterday I go to school.* ✅ *Yesterday I **went** to school.*
- **No capital letter for the date/days:** ❌ *monday, june* ✅ *Monday, June*
- **Forgetting sequence words**, so events feel jumbled. Use *first, then, finally*.
- **Writing 'Dear diary' without a comma:** ✅ *Dear Diary,*

sections.title: Memory Tip
sections.body: Remember the **3 D's of a diary: Date, Dear Diary, Day events.** And keep every verb in the **past** — a diary is written *after* the day is over.

sections.title: Practice
sections.body:
1. Put these into the past: I (wake) ______ up, I (eat) ______ breakfast, I (go) ______ to school.
2. Add a sequence word: "______ I brushed my teeth. ______ I had breakfast."
3. Write the date for today correctly.

**Answers:** 1. woke, ate, went  2. First / Then (e.g. First I brushed my teeth. Then I had breakfast.)  3. Saturday, 27 June 2026

sections.title: Key Vocabulary
sections.body: Words for diary writing.

glossary.definition: a personal book where you write about your daily life; a journal.
one piece of writing in a diary, usually for one day.
the order in which things happen, one after another.
the things you usually do every day in the same order.
to think carefully about something that happened.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
- A **diary** records your daily life; write one **entry** per day.
- Start with the **date** and **Dear Diary,**.
- Use the **past tense** for events that already happened.
- Use **sequence words** (first, then, after that, finally) to order events.
- End with how you **felt**.

flashcards.front: What tense do we mostly use in a diary?
flashcards.back: The simple past tense (I went, I felt).
First, then, after that, next, finally (any three).

flashcards.front: What do we write at the top of a diary entry?

flashcards.back: a personal book where you write about your daily life
one day's piece of writing in a diary

questions.prompt: Which tense do we mostly use to write a diary?
questions.explanation: A diary describes things that already happened, so we use the simple past.

questions.prompt: Which word shows the LAST event?
questions.explanation: 'Finally' is used for the last event in a sequence.

options: Yesterday I go to the market.
Yesterday I went to the market.
Yesterday I going to the market.
Yesterday I goes to the market.
questions.explanation: With 'yesterday' we use the past tense: went.

questions.prompt: What usually comes FIRST in a diary entry?
questions.explanation: A diary entry begins with the date at the top.

options: one piece of writing, usually for one day
questions.explanation: An entry is one day's piece of writing in a diary.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is best for a diary and grammatically correct?
options: Today is a busy day and I go to school.
Today was a busy day, and I went to school.
Today was a busy day and I go to school.

chapters.title: Land Conservation
chapters.description: Learn about protecting the land and use the future tense with 'will' and 'going to'.

lessons.title: Land Conservation and the Future Tense
lessons.summary: Learn how to protect the land and use 'will' and 'going to' to talk about future plans and predictions.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
**Land conservation** means protecting the soil, trees, and water so the land stays healthy for the future. In Ethiopia, people plant trees and build **terraces** to stop **soil erosion**.

When we talk about the **future** — our plans and what we think will happen — we use **will** and **going to**.

sections.title: What You Will Learn
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Use vocabulary about **the environment** and **conservation**.
- Use **will** for predictions and quick decisions.
- Use **going to** for plans and clear evidence.
- Talk about future actions to protect the land.

sections.title: The Future Tense: will and going to
sections.body:
There are two common ways to talk about the future.

**1. will + base verb** — for predictions, promises, and decisions made *now*.
- *I think the trees **will grow** tall.* (prediction)
- *I **will help** plant trees tomorrow.* (decision/promise)
- Negative: *won't* (will not). *The soil **won't erode** if we plant grass.*

**2. (am/is/are) going to + base verb** — for plans already made and predictions based on evidence.
- *We **are going to plant** trees next week.* (a plan)
- *Look at those clouds — it **is going to rain**.* (evidence now)

Both are followed by the **base verb**: will **grow**, going to **plant**.

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.body:
Read this short plan:

*"Our school **is going to** start a tree-planting project. Next month, every student **will plant** five trees. We **are going to** build small terraces on the hill to stop erosion. If everyone helps, the land **will become** green again."*

- **is going to start / are going to build** = plans already decided.
- **will plant / will become** = predictions and future results.
- Every verb after them is in the **base form**.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.body:
- **Adding -s or -ed after will:** ❌ *He will plants.* ✅ *He **will plant**.*
- **Forgetting 'be' in 'going to':** ❌ *I going to help.* ✅ *I **am going to** help.*
- **'will' for a fixed plan you already made:** often *going to* is better. *We **are going to** plant trees (already planned).*
- **Wrong negative:** ❌ *He willn't come.* ✅ *He **won't** come.*

sections.title: Memory Tip
sections.body: **WILL = a quick decision or a guess. GOING TO = an existing plan or clear evidence.** If you already decided before now, say *going to*. If you decide while speaking, say *will*.

sections.title: Practice
sections.body:
Choose 'will' or 'going to'.

1. Look at the sky! It ______ rain. ______
2. I promise I ______ help you plant trees. ______
3. We have a plan: we ______ clean the river on Saturday. ______
4. I think Ethiopia ______ have more forests in the future. ______
5. He ______ (not) cut that tree. ______

**Answers:** 1. is going to (evidence)  2. will (promise)  3. are going to (plan)  4. will (prediction)  5. won't / is not going to

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
- Use **will** + base verb for predictions, promises, and quick decisions.
- Use **going to** + base verb for plans and predictions with evidence.
- The negative of *will* is **won't**.
- **Land conservation** (planting trees, building **terraces**) protects soil from **erosion**.

chapters.title: Volunteerism
chapters.description: Learn about helping the community and use the present perfect tense.

lessons.title: Volunteerism and the Present Perfect Tense
lessons.summary: Learn about volunteering to help others and use the present perfect tense for experiences and recent actions.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
A **volunteer** is someone who helps other people **without being paid**. Students often **volunteer** to clean their school, plant trees, or help elderly neighbours. This is called **volunteerism**.

To talk about things you **have done** in your life (your experiences), we use the **present perfect tense**.

sections.title: What You Will Learn
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Use vocabulary about **volunteering** and **community**.
- Form the **present perfect** (have/has + past participle).
- Use it for **life experiences** and **recent actions**.
- Use *ever, never, already, yet, since, for* correctly.

sections.title: The Present Perfect Tense
sections.body:
We form the **present perfect** with **have / has + past participle**.

- I/you/we/they → **have** + past participle: *I **have helped**.*
- he/she/it → **has** + past participle: *She **has helped**.*

**Past participle:** regular verbs add **-ed** (help → helped). Irregular verbs change (do → **done**, see → **seen**, be → **been**, give → **given**).

**We use the present perfect for:**
1. **Life experiences** (no exact time): *I **have visited** Lalibela.* Often with *ever / never*: *Have you **ever volunteered**?*
2. **Recent actions** with a result now: *She **has just finished** the work.* Often with *already / yet*.
3. **Unfinished time** with *for* and *since*: *He **has worked** here **for** two years.* / *...**since** 2024.*

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.body:
Read about a volunteer club:

*"Our club **has helped** many people this year. We **have planted** 200 trees and **have cleaned** the river twice. Bethel **has already collected** clothes for the poor. I **have never felt** so proud. **Have** you **ever volunteered** in your community?"*

- **has helped / have planted** = experiences this year.
- **has already collected** = a recent action (with *already*).
- **have never felt** = a life experience (with *never*).

Use **for** + a length of time (*for two years*) and **since** + a starting point (*since 2024*).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.body:
- **Using past simple with 'ever/never':** ❌ *Did you ever visit Axum?* (less natural) ✅ *Have you **ever visited** Axum?*
- **Wrong participle:** ❌ *I have went.* ✅ *I have **gone**.*
- **for vs since:** ❌ *for 2024* ✅ *since 2024*; ❌ *since two years* ✅ *for two years*.
- **has with I/you/we/they:** ❌ *They has helped.* ✅ *They **have** helped.*

sections.title: Memory Tip
sections.body: **HAVE/HAS + 3rd form (past participle).** And remember: **FOR + a length of time** (for 2 years), **SINCE + a point in time** (since Monday). 'Since' points back to *when it started*.

sections.title: Practice
sections.body:
Complete with the present perfect.

1. I ______ (clean) the classroom already.
2. ______ you ever ______ (help) an old person?
3. She ______ (live) in Bahir Dar for five years.
4. We ______ (not / finish) the project yet.
5. They ______ (plant) many trees since 2023.

**Answers:** 1. have cleaned  2. Have ... helped  3. has lived  4. have not (haven't) finished  5. have planted

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
- The **present perfect** = **have/has + past participle**.
- Use it for **life experiences** (ever/never) and **recent actions** (already/yet).
- **for** + length of time; **since** + starting point.
- A **volunteer** helps the **community** without pay.

chapters.title: Fitness
chapters.description: Learn about keeping healthy and use adverbs of frequency.

lessons.title: Fitness and Adverbs of Frequency
lessons.summary: Learn how to stay fit and healthy and use adverbs of frequency to say how often you do things.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
**Fitness** means keeping your body strong and healthy through **exercise** and good food. Students who run, play, and eat well stay fit.

To say **how often** you do something — every day, sometimes, or never — we use **adverbs of frequency**.

sections.title: What You Will Learn
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Use vocabulary about **health** and **fitness**.
- Use **adverbs of frequency** (always, usually, often, sometimes, never).
- Put these adverbs in the **correct place** in a sentence.
- Use *How often...?* questions and expressions like *twice a week*.

sections.title: Adverbs of Frequency
sections.body:
**Adverbs of frequency** tell us *how often* an action happens. From most to least often:

**always (100%) → usually → often → sometimes → rarely/seldom → never (0%)**

**Word order rule:**
1. **Before** the main verb: *I **always eat** breakfast.* / *She **never drinks** soda.*
2. **After** the verb **be**: *He **is usually** tired.* / *They **are often** late.*

**Frequency phrases** go at the **end** of the sentence:
- *I exercise **every day**.*
- *She plays football **twice a week**.*
- *We go running **once a month**.*

To ask, use **How often...?** *How often do you exercise?*

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.body:
Read about a fit student:

*"Dawit **always exercises** in the morning. He **usually runs** for thirty minutes. He **often plays** football after school and **sometimes swims** at the weekend. He **never eats** too much sugar. He **is always** full of energy. He trains **three times a week**."*

- Adverbs (always, usually, often, sometimes, never) come **before** the main verb.
- With **be**: *He **is always** full of energy* (adverb after *is*).
- The phrase *three times a week* goes at the **end**.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.body:
- **Adverb after the main verb:** ❌ *I eat always breakfast.* ✅ *I **always eat** breakfast.*
- **Adverb before 'be':** ❌ *She always is happy.* ✅ *She **is always** happy.*
- **Double negative with 'never':** ❌ *I don't never smoke.* ✅ *I **never** smoke.*
- **Putting frequency phrases in the middle:** ❌ *I twice a week play.* ✅ *I play **twice a week**.*

sections.title: Memory Tip
sections.body: **Adverb goes BEFORE the main verb, but AFTER 'be'.** Short rhyme: *"Before the verb, after the be."* And single-word adverbs (always, never) go in the middle; longer phrases (every day) go at the end.

sections.title: Practice
sections.body:
Put the adverb in the correct place.

1. (always) I ______ drink water after exercise. ______
2. (never) She ______ eats junk food. ______
3. (usually) He ______ is tired in the evening. ______
4. (twice a week) They play football ______. ______
5. Make a question: ______ do you exercise?

**Answers:** 1. I always drink...  2. She never eats...  3. He is usually tired...  4. ...twice a week  5. How often

sections.title: Key Vocabulary

in good health; not ill.
the kind of food a person usually eats.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
- **Adverbs of frequency** say how often: **always, usually, often, sometimes, never**.
- Put them **before the main verb** but **after 'be'**.
- **Frequency phrases** (every day, twice a week) go at the **end**.
- Ask with **How often...?**
- Stay fit with regular **exercise** and a healthy **diet**.

flashcards.back: Before the main verb: I always eat breakfast.

flashcards.front: Where does the adverb go with 'be'?

questions.explanation: 'Always' means 100% of the time — the most often.

chapters.title: Self-Expression
chapters.description: Learn to express feelings and opinions and use adjectives and linking words.

lessons.title: Self-Expression: Feelings, Opinions and Adjectives
lessons.summary: Learn how to express your feelings and opinions clearly using adjectives and linking words like because and so.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
**Self-expression** means sharing your **feelings**, **opinions**, and **ideas** with others. It is an important skill: it helps you say what you think and how you feel in a clear and polite way.

To do this well, we use **adjectives** (describing words) and **linking words** like *because* and *so* to give reasons.

sections.title: What You Will Learn
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Use **adjectives** to describe feelings and things.
- Use phrases to give **opinions** (I think..., In my opinion...).
- Use **linking words** (because, so, but) to give reasons.
- Express yourself politely and clearly.

sections.title: Expressing Feelings and Opinions
sections.body:
**1. Adjectives** describe nouns and feelings.
- Feelings: *happy, sad, angry, excited, nervous, proud, bored.*
- An adjective usually comes **before** the noun (*a **beautiful** song*) or **after** the verb *be* (*I am **happy***).

**2. Giving opinions** — useful phrases:
- *I think (that)...* / *I believe...* / *In my opinion...*
- *I agree* / *I disagree* (when responding to others).

**3. Linking words** join ideas and give reasons:
- **because** = gives a reason. *I am happy **because** I passed the exam.*
- **so** = gives a result. *I studied hard, **so** I passed.*
- **but** = shows a difference. *I like music, **but** I don't like loud noise.*

Tip: *-ed* adjectives describe how you **feel** (*I am **bored***); *-ing* adjectives describe the **thing** (*the lesson is **boring***).

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.body:
Read how Selam expresses herself:

*"**In my opinion**, music is wonderful. I feel **happy** when I sing **because** it helps me relax. I was **nervous** before the concert, **but** I felt **proud** afterwards. The audience was **excited**, **so** I sang another song."*

- **Adjectives:** happy, nervous, proud, excited.
- **Opinion phrase:** In my opinion...
- **Linking words:** because (reason), but (difference), so (result).

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.body:
- **Confusing -ed and -ing adjectives:** ❌ *I am boring.* (means *you* are boring!) ✅ *I am **bored**.* (you feel bored)
- **Adjective after the noun:** ❌ *a song beautiful* ✅ *a **beautiful** song*
- **Using 'because' and 'so' together:** ❌ *Because I was tired, so I slept.* ✅ *Because I was tired, I slept.* (use only one)
- **Plural adjective:** ❌ *two happys children* ✅ *two **happy** children* (adjectives never add -s)

sections.title: Memory Tip
sections.body: **-ED = how I FEEL, -ING = how the THING is.** *I am interested* (my feeling); *the book is interesting* (the thing). And remember: **'because' gives the reason; 'so' gives the result.**

sections.title: Practice
sections.body:
1. Choose the right adjective: The film was very (bored / boring) ______.
2. Choose: I am (excited / exciting) ______ about the trip.
3. Join with 'because': I was happy. I won the game. ______
4. Join with 'so': It was raining. We stayed inside. ______
5. Add an opinion phrase: "______ football is the best sport."

**Answers:** 1. boring  2. excited  3. I was happy because I won the game.  4. It was raining, so we stayed inside.  5. I think / In my opinion

sections.title: Key Vocabulary

to say or show what you think or feel.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
- **Self-expression** means sharing your feelings and **opinions** clearly.
- **Adjectives** describe nouns and feelings (and never add -s).
- **-ed** adjectives = how you feel; **-ing** adjectives = how the thing is.
- **Linking words:** *because* (reason), *so* (result), *but* (difference).
- Give opinions with **I think...** or **In my opinion...**

chapters.title: Computer Development
chapters.description: Learn about computers and technology and use the passive voice.

lessons.title: Computer Development and the Passive Voice
lessons.summary: Learn about computers and technology and use the passive voice to describe how things are made and used.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
**Computers** have changed the world. They are used in schools, banks, and hospitals. The growth of computers over time is called **computer development**.

When we describe how things **are made** or **are used** — and the *doer* is not important — we use the **passive voice**: *Computers **are used** everywhere.*

sections.title: What You Will Learn
sections.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- Use vocabulary about **computers** and **technology**.
- Understand the difference between **active** and **passive** voice.
- Form the **passive** in the present and past.
- Use the passive to describe processes and facts.

sections.title: The Passive Voice
sections.body:
In an **active** sentence, the subject *does* the action:
- *People **use** computers.* (subject = people, the doer)

In a **passive** sentence, the subject *receives* the action. We use it when the doer is unknown or not important.
- *Computers **are used** by people.* / *Computers **are used** everywhere.*

**How to form the passive: be + past participle.**
- **Present passive:** *am/is/are* + past participle. *The data **is stored** on a computer.*
- **Past passive:** *was/were* + past participle. *The first computer **was built** long ago.*

We can add **by** to show the doer if needed: *The program **was written by** an engineer.*

Remember the **past participle**: regular verbs add **-ed** (use → used); irregular verbs change (write → **written**, build → **built**, make → **made**).

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.body:
Compare active and passive:

- Active: *Engineers **make** computers.* → Passive: *Computers **are made** by engineers.*
- Active: *Someone **invented** the internet.* → Passive: *The internet **was invented**.*

A short passive description:
*"Today, computers **are used** in almost every office. Information **is stored** safely. The first electronic computer **was built** in the 1940s. Now, programs **are written** all over the world."*

Every passive verb = **be + past participle**: are used, is stored, was built, are written.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.body:
- **Forgetting 'be':** ❌ *Computers used everywhere.* ✅ *Computers **are used** everywhere.*
- **Wrong participle:** ❌ *The letter was write.* ✅ *The letter was **written**.*
- **Wrong form of 'be':** ❌ *The data are stored* (for one thing) ✅ *The data **is stored**.*
- **Using passive when active is clearer:** keep it simple — use passive only when the doer is unknown or unimportant.

sections.title: Memory Tip
sections.body: **PASSIVE = BE + 3rd form (past participle).** Ask: *Who or what receives the action?* Put it first. If you don't know (or don't care) who did it, the passive is perfect.

sections.title: Practice
sections.body:
Change to the passive.

1. People use computers in schools. → Computers ______ in schools.
2. Engineers built the first computer. → The first computer ______ by engineers.
3. Someone writes new programs every day. → New programs ______ every day.
4. They store the data safely. → The data ______ safely.
5. People speak English worldwide. → English ______ worldwide.

**Answers:** 1. are used  2. was built  3. are written  4. is stored  5. is spoken

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
- The **passive voice** = **be + past participle**.
- Use it when the **doer** is unknown or not important.
- **Present passive:** is/are + participle; **past passive:** was/were + participle.
- Add **by** to show the doer if needed.
- **Computers** and **technology** are used everywhere today.
